utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties had a preliminary matter to be raised. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have two matters, both of which are connected to translation issues that arose yesterday. The first is related to P466, former 65 ter 05980. The issue arose in the first paragraph. The reference to the 6th Infantry Brigade has been corrected, as we discussed yesterday, to the 6th Infantry Battalion. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under document ID 0427-6215-0ET. And as usual if there is no objection, we would ask that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the existing translation with the revised version. The second issue relates, Mr. President, to document P190, 65 ter 02907, and that was the issue that arose in connection with the translation in the first paragraph for the word "organizovati." Now as it turns out, our inquiry with the translation service revealed that that word under its dictionary usage supports such terms as "start," or "launch." On the other hand, the specific term used in the translation, "set up," is not one of those terms listed, and in that connection I would note that the word "establish" appeared in the translation provided by the Karadzic Defence in the statement. So it's a reflection of how the term "organizovati" supports that kind of term but not technically. So the translation service's solution was to suggest the substitution of the word "organise," which is a much more literal and direct translation, I understand, of the B/C/S word. While that -- while it may contain the same ambiguity I just mentioned and that exists in the word "organise" in the English as well, at least it doesn't have the purported resolution of that ambiguity by the substitution of the term "establish," which is only susceptible of one meaning. So that's the solution to that interpretation or translation issue as suggested by the translation service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite understanding. Are the translation services suggesting that we change the word "organise" or we change the word "establish"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The term in B/C/S was "organizovati."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Organise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which we can't change?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. That stays, of course. And so that's the term used in the statement signed off on by the witness. It's also the term used in P190. And it was interpreted in the statement as "established," interpreted in P190 as "set up." As I indicated, while the B/C/S word supports words such as "start" or "launch" which are basically synonyms in that context, they consider -- it doesn't support the word or it's not the word "establish" is not technically listed, so they considered that the best solution would be to provide a much more direct use of that word. So they use the word "organise" as the interpretation of "organizovati," and that's what we've provided in the revised document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they're suggesting that we substitute "establish" or "set up" with "start" or "launch"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, they did not suggest that. They considered that if they simply I -- I agree that could have been an expedient, but I'm just relating what they provided and that was to use the word "organise." I would only say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Organise."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- in the English use of "organise," that is also susceptible of the meaning "start" or "launch" and carry through with the arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. This is just "organise." Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. So that appears in -- under doc ID 0427-6217-0ET. And when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been uploaded with the translation "organise" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in that doc ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And because I have hard copies of the old version, I'll do my best, if I'm referring to either the statement or P190, to remind myself that we've made that substitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comment Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I should do it, comment on this. We would agree that it's the same word, "organise," "organizovati," so there is no need for any elaborate translation. We agree that "organise" should be used as a translation for "organizovati."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then it should be uploaded with that word --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we don't have any objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Therefore, Madam Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the translation of -- into the English language of P466 by the newly uploaded ID 0427-6215-0ET, and you're similarly instructed to replace the existing translation of P190 by the newly uploaded document ID 0427-6217-0ET. For the Defence, I do understand that there may be a scheduling issue, scheduling matter, but you'd like not to raise it now or would you like to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's better -- I forgot good morning, Your Honours, the first time -- in the first place. Yeah, maybe it would be better to postpone that address until the end of the day since we would have more concrete answers from the Prosecution at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind that you you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Tieger will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday we ended the day discussing an aspect of the document P190.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's your order of the 31st of May, 1992. Which, among other things, orders in item 1: "Organise a camp in Vlasenica and provide security for it in the spirit of international rules." Now, yesterday there was a discussion, General, about the difference between "establishing" and "organising," a point you took pains to draw to our attention, and indeed you made that same claim to the Belgrade Court when you testified in the Grujic and Pavlovic case in 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that to mean or to be an assertion that essentially the Susica camp that existed in June and July and August and September of 1992 was the -- the same -- existed in that way in May of 1992 before you issued this order. That's essentially your claim, sir, that you were dealing with the same facility and you simply made an order regarding limited aspects of that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in order -- in -- in your effort to corroborate your claim that the camp as it later existed -- pre-existed or pre-dated your May 31st order, you told the Belgrade Court that The Hague Tribunal held a trial regarding this camp where the camp commander was convicted where witness statements show that this camp was established before the establishment of the brigade. So that was your claim to the Belgrade Court, correct, General, that The Hague Tribunal in the case of the camp commander, actually, the commander of the guards, Nikolic, had established that the Susica camp pre-existed your order? That was your claim; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a collection centre and at the same time it was a camp from the moment when on the 21st Vlasenica was liberated and when on the 19th an order was issued for disarmament and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but my question was not about your position on the circumstances pre-dating your order but more directly about whether or not you told the Belgrade Court that The Hague Tribunal had established the proposition you were advancing; that is, that the Susica camp pre-existed the order of late -- your order of late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, but I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I can -- let me quote you directly and see if you accept it, otherwise I'll put it on the screen. The quote is and appears in 65 ter 32499 at pages 60 to 61 of the English transcript and 33 of the Serbian: "Yes, yes, but I am telling you the operations officer made an error. It is a camp. It can be -- after all, The Hague Tribunal held a trial regarding this camp in Vlasenica where the camp commander was convicted, where witness statements show that this camp was established before the establishment of the brigade." Do you accept that -- that was your position to the Belgrade Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the statement made by Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the speaker. Could other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the microphone be adjusted. Could the usher assist. I don't know whether part of the answer was lost on not. I leave it in your hands, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's sufficient as it appears there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- the interpreters then confirmed that part of the answer was lost. Could you please repeat your answer. You said: "Yes, on the basis of the statement made by Nikolic," and what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikolic, Dragan who was convicted as camp commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be sure, you say that's the -- what the statement of Nikolic revealed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not necessarily the same as what was established by the court. Mr. Tieger, I leave it to you to further explore the matter if there's any need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fact is, General, the contrary is the case, that -- and here's the exchange that took place between Judge Schomburg and the accused Nikolic. This appears at 65 ter 32508, page 180 from the hearing of September 4th, 2003. "The Serb forces initially" -- this is Judge Schomburg speaking. "The Serb forces initially held the arrested Muslims and other non-Serbs either at a local school or the local prison in Vlasenica. In approximately late May or early June 1992, the Serb forces established a detention camp at Susica, the main detention facility in the Vlasenica area, and sent the arrested Muslims and non-Serbs there. Susica camp was run by the military and the local police militia. The camp guards were generally soldiers from the local area." And the accused responded: "Correct, Your Honour." The judge also said: "Susica camp was located approximately 1 kilometre from the town of Vlasenica, in a military facility that had previously been used for storage of military equipment. Men, women, and children were kept in the camp; however, the women and children generally stayed for only short periods of time before being forcibly transferred to nearby Muslim areas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for clarity, all the quotations from a certain document read into the transcript by Judge Schomburg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my understanding and then confirmed this -- that proposition -- both of those propositions, and if I continue then Nikolic also confirmed that, saying: "Correct, Your Honour." Both propositions were confirmed by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But can you help us to understand from which document Judge Schomburg was reading and quoting? Was it the plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Mr. President, but I can double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I indicated earlier that the -- Judge Schomburg read out the text of the plea, so that is my understanding, but I can certainly have that confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, General, contrary to your assertion that -- to the Belgrade Court, and here again, that the commander of the guards at Susica confirmed your proposition that it was a camp before, we can see that just the opposite is true, that Nikolic confirmed that the camp was established in late May or early June, that is consistent with the timing of your order, and that previously it had been used for storage of military equipment; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, you've been asked me about the camp all the time, and I have been trying to explain to you that the army had nothing whatsoever to do with the camp. And all the time -- well, it was the Crisis Staff that governed the crisis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to stop and start again. It is very hard to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're speaking too quickly. Therefore, you're invited to start --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all the time, there's an attempt to move my order through the camp. However, the Susica camp was not under the army. On my order, the army only secured the camp by way of the guards service. As for the running of the camp itself, that was under the Crisis Staff, the Ministry of Interior; specifically, the centre of public security from Vlasenica. The commander of the camp is a policeman from the police station. His deputy is from the police station. The commander of the camp who was appointed by -- by the commander of the special unit was Mr. Nikolic. So the army is nowhere there. I ordered the battalion commander to secure the camp, but the camp, the facilities where they are put up, the materiel, the personnel, the POWs, according to information received. So please let us make a distinction there. So the army had absolutely nothing to do with the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- apart from guarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from guarding the camp. It was only guarding the camp. Through my order, I ordered that an assessment be made, that a paper be drawn up, and that security be established. In that paper and in that order, there is no mention of Dragan Nikolic, there is no mention of Basic, who was allegedly the warden, then Risto Vidovic is not there either. So the army did not appoint them. And I don't know why all this time this is being imputed to me, this order, the camp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't worry about why parties are putting questions to you. Mr. Tieger will now put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you have claimed a couple of times the army had absolutely nothing to do with the camp apart from guarding the camp, is what you've said. So let's set aside guarding the camp, for a moment, as part of your organisation of the Susica camp. The army also ordered operative interviews of the prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally ordered that. That is to say, that the security organ from the battalion, the 4th Battalion, should conduct interviews, operative interviews, and that indispensable information should be provided to the chief of the security services in the command. However every military conscript or, rather, every POW that the gentlemen interviewed, the gentleman from the battalion, he returned every such person as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That actually anticipated my next question. Your chief of security and related officials also took people out of the camp for interviews. That's correct, too?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But you know on whose orders? Do you? Who could have ordered that, to have prisoners taken out? Did anybody ask the commander of the brigade or the commander of the battalion? No. The chief of the public security centre was the one who had the power to allow that, namely, to have prisoners of war taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he allow that or did he order that? You said on whose orders, now you say "allowed." Did he allow it or did he order it, the chief of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief had the right on the basis of the statements made by the mentioned Mr. Nikolic. I hadn't studied this. And I quote, he said: "The army was there just on paper and they had no say. All decisions were made by the Crisis Staff and the public security station and the security -- and the special police." So the army did not have any powers whatsoever except for guard services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what are you quoting from Drago Nikolic? Is that his testimony or is that his statement or is it something he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't say that to me. I read that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the statement? I heard translation that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that we're receiving B/C/S on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general terms, would you tell us what you personally observed and what you -- and not recount what you read in statements of other persons? To the extent these statements are in evidence, we will evaluate them, but we are expecting you to tell us what you know from your personal experience, your personal observation. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in light of that response, Mr. President, I'm going to tender 65 ter 32508 which is the relevant portion of the sentencing hearing that I read out before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we still --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think we still have to decide on the admission of P7356, which is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I want to take a look at how the, quote/unquote, organisation of the camp in Susica went after your order. First of all, within a matter of weeks, there were many hundreds of Muslim prisoners held in Susica. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those included not only men but women and sometimes children; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The women and the children were not imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, they were brought to the camp and during their stay in the camp, they were not free to leave. They were held in the camp for that period. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the beginning, we said that the Susica facility was an asylum, a temporary kind of asylum not only for Muslims but also for Serbs, so along with prisoners there were civilians there too. Specifically in Vlasenica on the 21st, what happened was that people were going there to spend the night with their family, and then in the morning the authorities would organise it for them so they could go to Kladanj or wherever else they wanted to. That's the truth. Why would anyone want to capture women and children? And for them, it was a place of safety. They asked to go there because that's where they were safe. It was for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, these people, the men and the women, were considered prisoners; correct? And they were referred to as such by the Bosnian Serb military authorities. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They were not prisoners. If you take my report to the East Bosnia Corps command where I am asking that the prisoners of war are urgently relocated - urgently - and that the brigade command was not responsible for organising the camp that was at the level of the corps command, the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to the East Bosnia Corps, when they looked at the situation in the brigade, also instructed the command of the East Bosnia Corps to urgently organise the camp. After those orders, in late June, 400 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, please stop. Let's take this sequentially, please. I asked you whether they were referred to as such - that is, prisoners - by the Bosnian Serb military authorities. You said no. Then you began a lengthy explanation of what you considered to be relevant orders relating to Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me look -- let me call up P353, page 232 in the English and 230 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. This is a meeting, and we can go back, dated -- we don't have to move. Dated the 25th of June, 1992, reflected in General Mladic 's notebook. It's a meeting in Vlasenica, as we can see, at 1630. And there the president of the municipality, Milenko Stanic, states: "Over 800 prisoners," prisoners, "200 of whom are women and children who were brought last night, pose a problem." Now that's a reflection, General, of the understanding that the people who were brought into these detention facilities were, in fact, being detained, irrespective of whether they were ultimately going to be sent to Kladanj or held for further operative interviews, sent to Batkovic, or indeed suffer an even worse fate.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those civilians, complete families, would come, and you can imagine, the Serbs went to visit them as well and brought them gifts. Had this been a classic prison or a camp, according to the rules nobody would be able to approach it. However, their Serb neighbours were bringing them food. And as soon as the municipality provided transport and buses, those civilians went to Kladanj, Zivinice, Cerska, or wherever they said they wanted to go. I mean, it's a burden for the municipality to hold so many people without proper conditions and insufficient food, so who would do this reasonably in such conditions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm going to ask you about what -- some of what you now appear to tell us you knew about the operative details of what was happening in Susica camp. So let's turn to P193, which is a report by the then-commander of the Vlasenica Battalion, Major Slobodan Pajic, who later became your assistant commander for logistics. Now this is a report, as you can see, an assessment of the danger to buildings in Susica from attacks on them and to the units from attack from them. And it's dated at the front June of 1992 and signed and stamped by Pajic on the second page, indicating that work must be completed by the 17th of June. So that's -- 1992. So that's the time-period. And if we can turn to page 4 of the English, and I believe the same page in the Serbian, Pajic provides the following: "In order to prevent informing the public about the prisoners' appearance and the conditions they live in, any attempts to take recording devices and explosives inside or conduct interviews must be prevented, extensive movement must be prohibited, and so on. Visits of any type must be prohibited, particularly bringing food and other material to the prisoners." General, contrary to the assertions you just made regarding the benign and almost philanthropic attitude toward the prisoners at Susica, your subordinates were aware of the conditions, sought to ensure they would not be revealed to the public or media, and, indeed, sought to prevent food from being brought to these prisoners. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you read who it was there. This is a proposal for the report of the members of the commission and the report was drafted on the basis of my order. The order then goes to the commander. And then the commander ultimately wrote the order on the basis of the report. So this is a commission putting forward a proposal. And then later you can see what the commander decided. So this is a proposal for security that was to be provided, and there is no question about managing the camp or the camp premises. Only security. There is no warden there or any camp staff. It's only the security there. You have three guards' posts and four guards who are securing the warehouse in view of the fact that the camp is at the warehouse -- in the warehouse. I am telling you what I heard, that people would come and they would bring -- I mean, there are statements by witnesses also. Simply speaking, these were neighbours who would then come and bring the food early in the morning, and then once the transport was arranged, they would leave. I don't know what you're asking from me. I mean, you're looking at me so you can tell me what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, based on what you've just told us, it appears that you were very much aware of the conditions in the camp that your subordinates were guarding, and so you must have been aware that the condition of these -- the condition in which these prisoners lived and the treatment they received was horrific; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, the whole time you're referring to the order, and you're trying to do something that has nothing to do with anything, I never entered the camp, once. My area of responsibility stretched to 150 kilometres. I never entered the camp except after the war when I was the commander of the 5th Corps. Therefore, my information about the camp is minimal. I had an assistant. I had a commander for morale and religious affairs who, on the 3rd of July, became a member of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War. Therefore, my information in the course of the war was very superficial. It was very, very slight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you just told us in respect of the Pajic assessment that you commissioned that. He says in there, "Let's not anybody know about the condition of the prisoners." So I'm asking you now whether you claim that you did not know what the condition of the prisoners was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't read the document to the end. First of all, this is something that the commission proposed. Pajic didn't say that. Thirdly, the proposal was not handed to the brigade commander. Sir, you can see to whom the draft was provided to, to the guards duty and the battalion, not to the commander of the brigade. You really need to read it to the end. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let's -- let's be direct. Number one: Do you deny or confirm or say you don't know that conditions in the Susica camp - lack of food, abysmal hygiene, beatings, rapes, killings - was -- prevailed in Susica in -- after the time of -- of your May 31st order?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think this is becoming ridiculous. Throughout the whole time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you're talking about my order, but I'm telling you as far as the camp -- the whole time, you're talking about my order. I don't know what you're objective is. We're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, it's not for you to decide whether we are wasting time or not. Second, you're invited to listen carefully to what Mr. Tieger put to you. The only thing he did, he referred to the time after your order. That is, time. That is, after the 31st of May. There was no other direct link suggested at this moment by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you please, I'm telling you the whole time that the army didn't have any authority or responsibility for the camp, so why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The question was whether you deny or confirm or say you don't know that the conditions in Susica camp - and Mr. Tieger mentioned a few, one of them lack of food - whether you deny or confirm that that was the prevailing situation in Susica camp. Do you deny? Do you confirm? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my information is that the municipality and the town of Vlasenica were in danger in view of a large number of prisoners and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- people who had moved out. I will give you an answer immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you should start giving me an answer. And if we need further explanations, we'll ask for it. Do you deny or do you confirm or do you not know that the conditions in Susica camp were as they were portrayed by Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. All I know is that there were too many and that I sent a request to the East Bosnia Corps command that had to do with the situation in Vlasenica to relocate the prisoners of war to the Batkovic camp as soon as possible. So at the briefing I was told that there was a large number of these people, and the municipality simply could not support accommodation and food for them. And so on the basis of that, a request was drafted to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you earlier told us that there was not sufficient food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you didn't understand me, that I didn't have sufficient conditions for such a large number of refugees; 3.000 to 4.000 refugees in Vlasenica. Then prisoners of war. The pressure was great. And so they were asking me along the chain of command to unburden the Vlasenica municipality and to relocate the prisoners of war, and this is what I did. Even the General Staff ordered this to the Eastern Bosnia Corps to organise the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For one reason or another, you're not answering my question. My question simply was whether you told us a minute ago that food was not sufficient and that it was a burden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that I did say that, but I meant the entire municipality. I didn't mean the prisoners of war. I meant the entire municipality. Because the 4.000 refugees were a burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me then read to you what you said. You said: "I mean, it's a burden for the municipality to hold so many people without proper conditions and insufficient food," which seems to confirm that the conditions were not proper and that there was insufficient food. And that was what Mr. Tieger asked you, whether you can confirm that or not. But you told us already --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There wasn't enough food. Not only for the prisoners of war. I just want to broaden that. It affected the entire population because 4.000 refugees arrived in the meantime, so the president of the municipality was asking me to relocate them because they just could not cope with so many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were aware that there was not sufficient food in Susica camp. There may have not been sufficient food for others as well, but you were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about Susica, no. Generally there was a shortage of food. Generally. But he asked that we relocate the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "There wasn't enough food," and you said this two minutes ago, "not only for the prisoners of war," and you wanted to broaden that. That means that you were aware that there was not sufficient food for the prisoners of war and, as you broadened the matter, also not for others. So you were aware of the insufficiency of food available at Susica camp. That's what you told us a second ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I did say it, but I was not in a position to know, because I was never in the camp, I wasn't receiving the information, so -- well, here, I accept that I said that. I never received information about the camp, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I say "please proceed," but I shouldn't have said that in view of the clock. Mr. Andric, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue, Mr. Andric. My I advise you that you should always make clear what you know from your personal observation and what you know by analysing statements of others, which you're not invited to do. We're interested in what you know by your own observation. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a last question, General, about the Muslim prisoners in Susica. These hundreds of prisoners who swelled the facility and whose presence triggered the request for a corps-level facility like Batkovic, these were all people who were captured by the army and police and then held in Susica; right.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the army capture people, Muslims, who were then held as prisoners in Susica?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You spoke in general terms, Mr. Prosecutor, because half an hour ago you said that in Susica there were women and children. So the army did not take women and children prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that wasn't the question. You're intelligent enough to understand the question. The question was whether the army captured people, Muslims, who were then held in Susica. Men not excluded in that question. So would you refrain from reminding Mr. Tieger of what he asked and would you please answer the question. Were there -- did the army capture people, Muslims, who were then held as prisoners in Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army, the police, the Territorial Defence, and all structures of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about them? Did they capture people who were then held as prisoners in Susica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said to you that able-bodied military-aged men who had committed a crime who had taken part in armed conflicts or in some other way aided the Muslim side, they were the ones who were taken to the camp. Now, all the others who did not do that were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, even if you're released you must have been captured before. That's one. Second, the focus of the question was whether the military and the police captured people who were then held as prisoners in Susica. Did the military do that; and did the police do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A simple "yes" three questions ago would have done. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let's return more generally to the orders or decisions to move out the Muslims. That is, your 26 May order, your -- the 28 May order, the Birac SAO government decision. Now, these orders to move out the Muslims were expressions of the Bosnian Serb position that there needed to be fewer Muslims in Birac in order to draw borders on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer and come a bit closer to the microphone, which perhaps could be adjusted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you knew who Rajko Dukic [Realtime transcript read in error "Djukic"] was; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was the president of the republic-level SDS Executive Board; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. I just knew Rajko Dukic as the director of Boksit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you also know that he was co-ordinator - that is, the republic-level official - tasked with responsibility for SAO Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at P7081, and turn the page to item 4, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is the Executive Board recommending to the Main Board that in view of the formation of the assembly and the ministerial council that certain people should be responsible for "the accomplishment of regionalisation on the ground," and Mr. Dukic proposed for Birac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at P7082.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see the decision appointing Mr. Dukic, the president of the as the Executive Committee of the SDS BH, as the designated member co-ordinator for the SAO whose responsibilities are to report matters, become involved in the work of the Crisis Staff, carry out decisions of the assembly, and so on. So, General, you must have been aware that Mr. Dukic, a significant republic-level SDS official, was active in activities with the SAO Birac government with which you interacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The witness had answered in response to the previous question; namely, what he knew about the position of Rajko Dukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection denied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I see this. I didn't know. So a major, a brigade commander for seven municipalities, a short period of time to get to know everybody, that's impossible. So I know Mr. Dukic as an excellent businessman and the director of the Boksit mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's then look at what this -- what Mr. Dukic, the co-ordinator, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My I interrupt you for just one moment, Mr. Tieger. It's -- we always see in the transcript "Mr. Djukic" but I think it's clear from the documents and from what are you saying it's Mr. Dukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at what Mr. Dukic had to say about what was happening in Birac and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to P4581. That's a session of the Assembly, the Republika Srpska Assembly or the Assembly for the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in late July 1992. And if we could turn to page 71 and then quickly to page 72 of the English, page 73 of the B/C/S. Can you turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic begins first: "We are establishing the state." He goes on to say: "We are talking about borders," and then here's the quote: "We say that borders are drawn in the field. The people draw the borders. You must admit the state of facts." He goes on to talk about how the world would react if they -- if the Bosnian Serbs withdrew, and he says: "So the option is to take at least as much as belongs to us, and I will tell you that we have not even come close to that." Now, he goes on, talking about Bijeljina a bit, expressing concern about Muslim judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he says: "So I'm asking you gentlemen why we expelled all Muslim judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik." Then he goes on to talk about Birac. "If we move further there is Birac which is 100 to 108 kilometres away and has 120.000 Muslims, that is how many there were but I hope that has at least been halved, and 90.000 Serbs." Now, there, General, Mr. Dukic, the republic-level emissary to the SAO Birac, is clearly expressing the view before the Bosnian Serb Assembly that the reduction of the Muslim population is necessary, desirable, and is, in fact, being effected; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. This is the first time I see this and I do not wish to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You saw that he talked about borders being drawn in the field; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that here, but he's the one who should be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a reference to taking control of areas that might otherwise be held by or allotted to the Muslims; correct? The taking control on the ground.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I really don't know why you're asking me about that. I don't know that at all. Not my document. I'm a soldier. I'm not a politician. So there's no need for me to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whenever a question is put to you, don't say that it shouldn't be asked. Just answer the question, if you can. If you know, tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well. But no comment on what questions should be put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there's no need for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are under an obligation to answer a question. Whether the answer is, I don't know, that's all fine, but to say "I don't have to answer that question" is incorrect. You are under an obligation to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, I repeat: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I presented you with what Mr. Dukic said before the entire assembly and before the Bosnian Serb leadership because you yourself, General, well understood that conquering non-Serb territory was exactly what was required and expected. And that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 1D04790, please. That was -- that became -- I had that exhibit number yesterday. D1036. And the transcript for that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see, General, this is a transcript of a video footage of you. And in fact, it's included in your statement as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After receiving applause, you state your favourite applause will be when the Serbian Bosnia is free, and: "... it will be when we are all equally involved in that struggle, the Serbian history will show, but I can tell you that never in the Serbian history we had such a chance to win. This brigade holds 70 per cent of the territory of SAO Birac compared to the 30 per cent that the enemy holds. According to that, just a little of effort is needed to retain those areas and to conquer more, then President Karadzic can go peacefully to the conference."

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would kindly ask to you have the entire text read out because this is just a portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, you are not telling any of the parties what they should read to you, yes or no. If there's any need to pay attention to other parts, then in re-examination the Defence will ask further questions and will consider other parts of this. Again - and this is the last time I'm warning - you should not tell the parties what they should ask you and what they should not ask you. If there's anything at this moment to intervene, Mr. Stojanovic will do that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time of this speech, General, Bosnian Serb forces had already taken such places as Seher, as we saw yesterday, Memici. That's correct, right? That's part of the 70 per cent you were talking about here.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I kindly ask now do allow me to explain. What you're doing has nothing to do with any of this. Now you mention Seher and we are in Milici. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, haven't I been clear enough to you? You're not in a discussion with Mr. Tieger. You're here to answer his questions. You're under an obligation to answer questions. If you don't, if you contumaciously refuse to answer questions or are not answering them, then you expose yourself to contempt of the court proceedings which can result in penalties. I again and now for the last time are telling you that you should not tell Mr. Tieger what he should ask. You just have to answer his questions. And again, you're undermining your own testimony if you continue to do this, and that is certainly not why the Defence had called you as a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last time, General. You refer in your speech to the fact that the brigade holds 70 per cent of the territory of SAO brigade. That 70 per cent that you're referring to in this speech included places like Seher and Memici; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made that speech on 25th of September, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when a Serb village under --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the answer is "yes"? I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir, but you're now proposing to make another speech. I asked a pretty simple question. You've now given the date. So the answer is that by that time, by the time -- this speech, when you're referring to the brigade holding 70 per cent of the territory, that includes the villages I mentioned. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, since you say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not correct because Mr. Tieger says so. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now you also mention that in exhorting your audience toward further efforts and more conquering, that that would enable President Karadzic to go peacefully to the conference. That means so that he could go to the peace conference and present the negotiators with fait accompli about territories that were held and then claim that those new realities could not be ignored and should be incorporated into the settlement of what constituted Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask you something. Could I kindly ask you something? I mean, I simply feel the urge to say this to you. The consequence of this speech, please, I'm kindly ask you this. This makes no sense. I was making this speech to women and children because Milici was falling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asked you to whom you made that speech. You're simply asked whether what you told your audience, whoever that may have been, is that you -- if I could interpret your words, Mr. Tieger, you paved the way for more successful negotiations by -- on the ground getting under your control certain territories. If that's true, tell Mr. Tieger; if you disagree, tell Mr. Tieger as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree that this was said as a consequence of the talks. On the contrary, the motivation of people to send their able-bodied military conscripts to defend Milici because Milici was under threat and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I did not assert to you that your speech was a consequence of the talks. I referred instead to a particular reference you made during your speech and asked you to confirm its meaning. So in light of that, let me present you with something that Dr. Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 02406; English page 157, B/C/S page 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic offering there at the 46th Assembly Session a retrospective, stating: "We have created new realities," and then gives an example, "speaking," he says, "in narrow terms, Zvornik used to be 60-40 to the advantage of the Muslims, but the Serbs from Zenica came, they occupied Kozluk, the Muslims left for Europe and I do not know where else. And then those gentlemen told us who gives you a right to ask for Zvornik? We request Zvornik based on the right which comes out of a new reality. This are war has created the new reality. There are now the Serbs from Zenica there. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims then you have to wage a new war in order to expel these Serbs back to Zenica. We request Zenica according to this right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "We request Zvornik ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Zvornik, sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, that is an expression from the Supreme Commander about the use of the new realities created by territories taken by the Bosnian Serb forces in the course of their discussions with the internationals, and that is exactly what you're referring to in your speech before the people of Milici by telling them that with further conquering Dr. Karadzic can go peacefully to the conference. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that I was motivated by the people who were there to defend Milici, which was just the impetus, if possible. To preserve Milici, because Milici was about to fall. There were about 40.000 citizens there, Naser Oric destroyed a couple of villages, he had reached Milici, Vlasenica was under attack. What else could a commander say but to say something to motivate the fact? Anyway, according to the land register 70 per cent of the land in that area was Serb owned. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you ask rhetorically what else somebody could have said, and no one can know the answer to that in totality. We just know what you said and I'm focusing your attention or trying to do so on what your actual words were and what their meaning was. Now, if you don't want to answer my question about that and about its relationship to Dr. Karadzic's explanation of the utility of the new realities, then I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept in its entirety my speech. I accept my speech in its entirety. I mean, I accept it in its entirety, word for word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender 65 ter 2406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, how many pages is this document? You referred only to a few pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The entire session is quite a long one, and when I -- I should have specified the excerpt, which I believe is consistent with our practice. We can certainly indicate that this excerpt is admitted but have a document to which we can add further excerpts if they arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A number will be reserved, and we already decide that the relevant portions you read are admitted into evidence, but you have to administratively upload the portions you relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the cover page. And that all should be uploaded under number P7357. Mr. Tieger, could we receive, well, let's say within the next 48 hours the excerpt to be uploaded and you report in court under what doc ID that is uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up P353, page 246, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, I accepted my statement, my statement. I did. I accepted my statement but not the other documents, I mean. Just my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to accept anything. You testified that you accept your statement -- Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accepted my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Other documents, we decide on whether it will be admitted into evidence irrespective of whether you accept anything. And would you again refrain from your attempts to take over this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you see on the screen before you now it's a meeting that took place in Zvornik on 30th of June 1992 attended by a number of people, most notably including Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. You see some of the other participants on this first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So we saw Milenko Stanic, president of the SAO Birac government on the first page. Here we see the presence of Marko Pavlovic, also known as Branko Popovic, about whom we have spoken during the course of your testimony. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the name of Milenko Stanic is crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He also appears on the previous page, Mr. President, in his capacity as a Vlasenica municipality official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 248 of the English and 246 of the Serbian, we see remarks by Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he begins by reporting to Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic: "We have defined the western boundaries in the area of the Birac region." Now, he's talking about what we have already seen depicted in the maps we reviewed, and that's the movement of the borders of areas controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces into the previous Muslim municipality of Kalesija and the formation of the new Serbian municipality of Kalesija later called the Serbian municipality of Osmaci; right.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what date this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: June 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I say, Mr. Prosecutor, Kalesija was in the hands of the Serb forces from the 8th to the 10th of May. From the 8th to 10th of May. On the 23rd, the Muslims took Kalesija back, so it was under their military and political authority. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, you gave the order to the forces in Osmaci to move the Muslims. On the 27th of May, as we've seen, those forces came into Seher, for example, rounded the people up, separated the men from the women, took the men to detention facilities. We also discussed yesterday the taking of control over Memici, and we saw the map that embraced those areas. So those -- those efforts were all reflections of drawing the borders of the Birac region in the field; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just asked me about the documents, about Kalesija being under our control, and I am explaining that it wasn't, that the three villages that you mentioned - Seher, Like, and let me help you, and -- Seher, Like, and -- there's another village. It will come back to me. That was in the depth of the Serbian municipality of Osmaci. Three Serbian villages. So yesterday we were talking -- for your information, so that you know it precisely, there were 300 people in those villages. Out of those 300, 129 were taken to the school and then to the camp. And luckily all of them were brought back so -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, answer the question rather than to tell us what you consider relevant. If you don't answer those questions, we'll have to interpret what we see on our own without any answers to questions you have given. Mr. Tieger, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on and see what the other officials at the meeting reported to the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership. As we've seen, Branko Grujic was also there. And we'll look at his comments at page 249 in the English and 247 in the B/C/S in a moment. But before we do, I just want to confirm that you knew Mr. Grujic; correct? So in the course of establishing your brigade between the 19th of May and, let's say, the 2nd of June, you went to various municipalities and met with people, among others, him?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Grujic. I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you spoke with him and learned from him about his overriding desire to ensure that the Serb people were protected from their perceived enemies; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss that with Grujic. I met Grujic only when I came and we became friends later on. But I never talked about this with Grujic. I never had the opportunity because I was mostly in Sekovici, Osmaci, Zvornik. At that time, there was no fighting there because on 23rd of April all combat actions in Zvornik were over. So I was constantly along the axis of Zvornik and Kladovo and another one, so I didn't have time to have any contacts with him. I never spoke with him about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, at his trial in Belgrade, when you testified under oath, you vouched for him as a man -- "a man who, above all, wanted to protect the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that, just as I wanted it. But I don't think that neither of us wanted to commit genocide against another ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's exactly what you said to the Belgrade Court, isn't it, that it seemed to you he's not a man who is thinking about genocide. Even though he wasn't charged with genocide in that proceeding; right? You just thought to volunteer that information.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I should have done that or not. You can evaluate that, but ... that was my thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the fact is that contrary to what you've just told this Court, you did speak with Mr. Grujic. You told the Belgrade Court you spoke to him and as a result you were aware of the fact, according to you, that he was a man who, above all, wanted to protect the Serbian people; right? You learned at least that much from him. That's -- or do you now disavow your Belgrade testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't disavow anything that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the fact is that you did speak to Grujic. He's not a man who amassed his feelings about protecting the Serbian people or what that required, was he? He was open about that.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all spoke openly about the need to protect our own people. I don't know what is of dispute there. I don't know when he said that, but he did say that a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me show you what Mr. Grujic said candidly to a western media correspondent who was -- about what protecting the Serb people entailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we can turn to 65 ter 32503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, you said you all spoke openly about the need to protect our own people. I don't know when he said that but he did say that a number of times. Was that in conversations with you or...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met Mr. Grujic perhaps sometime in 1992 after the brigade was formed when I was touring the municipalities. So I don't recall when he said that to me. So I cannot confirm when he told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But he told you but you don't remember when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a confirmation that you -- he did tell you but you don't remember when he told you. Is that what you confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now a minute ago you told us that you never talked about this with Mr. Grujic and that you had no time even to speak with him about these matters. Now, two minutes later, you're telling us -- Witness, would you not interrupt me. Now, two minutes later, you're telling us that although you do not know when he told you that that's what he did tell you. May I remind you that it's not advised to change your testimony within one or two minutes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, we're looking at an article by Roger Cohen of the "New York Times" that appeared on March 7th, 1994. We do not have a B/C/S or Serbian translation at the moment, so I will have to read you the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do it slowly, please, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cohen begins by talking about Branko Grujic. Begins: "Up through a ghostly terrain of smashed and ransacked former Muslim homes, Branko Grujic led the way intent on showing off his crowning contribution to what he calls the victory of Serbian Orthodox Christianity over Islam in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where are you reading from so that that can be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the very top. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He goes on to note that Mr. -- that they arrive at the top of the summit of a cliff. Then he notes Mr. Grujic states: "The Turks destroyed the Serbian church that was here when they arrived in Zvornik in 1463. Now we are rebuilding the church and reclaiming this as Serbian land forever and ever." As we go down the page, he mentions Mr. Grujic's position. Where it begins the -- keep scrolling, please. The second fact is that Grujic is the most important official in a strategic town that lies on the border with Serbia and is also less than 20 miles from the front line to the west at Kalesija ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It continues: "Beyond the immediate conflict over Tuzla, Zvornik is important in a broader respect. Like other towns on the Drina including Foca and Visegrad, it was at least 50 per cent Muslim before the war and the Bosnian government wants the town back if a peace settlement is to be reached. This notion makes Grujic laugh. "'Return to Zvornik?', the mayor scoffed. 'The Muslims must be joking. This was a Serbian town before Islam existed in the Balkans. They'd better not dream of things they cannot fulfil or things will just get worse. Either a peace is worked out soon or we Serbs advance. We cannot standstill. Kalesija is Muslim now, but it may not be for long.'" And then continuing down to the bottom of the article, Grujic notes that he had renamed the Muslim village of Divic, Sveti Stefan, after the Christian Saint Steven, and finally notes: "We are liberating our beautiful land. Tell Serbs in America it is their duty to send us money for the church." Now, General, I put to you that Mr. Grujic's candor before a western journalist from a prominent publication reflects his openness in describing the objectives that resulted in the taking of territory, the conquering of territory, and that was equally open with you about what the objectives were and what needed to be done. That's the reality of your discussions with Mr. Grujic and your vouching for him in the Belgrade trial.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship between myself and Mr. Grujic was a friendly one during the war and after the war. However, I was the commander of the Birac Brigade and he was the commander [as interpreted] of the Zvornik Brigade, so that we didn't really met that often. It's my personal opinion which I stated that -- what I said about him is my personal opinion. I cannot comment on what is written here, because this is an article that I am seeing for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The transcript says that you identified him as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was the president of the municipality in the Zvornik Brigade. Of the Zvornik Brigade. That was the time when the Zvornik Brigade was formed, on the 2nd of June, 1992. So I had no authority over Zvornik, none at all. Only perhaps if I passed through Zvornik, I would drop by for a coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look next at what Mr. Grujic reported to the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership about what had been done in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But first I'd tender 65 ter 32503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32503 receives number P7358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections admitted into evidence. It should be marked for identification, as a matter of fact, because there's no translation yet, Mr. Tieger. So I made a mistake. P7358 is marked for identification awaiting a translation. However, no objections were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn to page 247 in the English, page 249 of the -- P353. I'm sorry. 247 of the Serbian and 249 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see Mr. Grujic speaking, and he says: "We have 32.000 Serbs. We have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk," if we turn the page in both languages. "... to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The page has gone away again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he also praises Marko Pavlovic. And we see Pavlovic's remarks on the next page. Let's take a look at those. And with respect to Pavlovic, you and he were on friendly terms, like comrades; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for the transcript, I think you started reading at e-court page 249 and then moved to e-court page 250 in the English, where the first line reads -- reads "with our children."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think for Mr. Pavlovic we are on e-court page 251.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn quickly then to 65 ter 32499. Page 36, please, and page 21 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is your testimony in the Belgrade trial. And here you're discussing Mr. Pavlovic. You indicate at the bottom of page 36 in the English that you met, you were on correct terms after that. You, as the commander of the Birac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're asked what period you're talking. You say in July or June. You were asked: "What sort of contact did you have? Business or private?" And you say: "Well, we were on friendly terms, like comrades." Now, you confirm that's what you said to the Belgrade Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I -- I don't receive interpretation because you have not switched on your microphone, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would kindly ask that we have the previous page in B/C/S. It seemed to me that the quotation was not proper. The Prosecutor asked the witness whether it is correct that he said that he had a friendly relationship with Pavlovic, and I would kindly ask that part of the question and answer be read out, the answer that the witness provided to the Special Court in Belgrade, precisely on this page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the previous page or on the page which we have on our screen now? Because Mr. Tieger, both in his question and then when reading it out, I think literally read what [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely the page that we have on the screen now, and I can say that it is the question put by the Presiding Judge, the third one from the bottom in B/C/S, and the third answer from the bottom in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is reading from the English. Could you seek assistance, Mr. Stojanovic, which part you think was misquoted? Because I'm unable to identify any misquote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to read this out without any intention of leading the witness in any way. The president is saying: "You became friends two times?" And Andric is saying: "Not friends but we did speak in a friendly way. I was never his superior" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what Mr. Tieger quoted. Mr. Tieger quoted -- and if it's not there in the B/C/S version, you can inform us. Mr. Tieger quoted the answer to a question put by the Presiding Judge, the question being: "What sort of a contact did you have? Business or private? " Then the witness is recorded as having answered: "Well, we were on friendly terms, like comrades." That's what included in his question and that what is he asked the witness about after that. If there's any reason to revisit the matter and to draw attention to other portions, you have an opportunity to do so in re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You should not have intervened if the quote is found also in the B/C/S version. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very simple, General Andric: Do you agree that you told the Belgrade Court, under oath, "we were on friendly term, like comrades"?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said was under oath, so friendship can be interpreted in several ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, this is a literal quote. Do you deny that you said it, or do you confirm that you said this? We're not seeking an interpretation. We're just establishing whether you used those words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Confirm that I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was it truth -- was it the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said if a person can be friends after two times -- well, we did not quarrel, we did not really communicate. He was not my subordinate. I was not his superior, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is was it the truth, the one sentence you uttered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that it was the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you were -- when you were asked by Mr. Tieger just a few minutes ago -- and let me find it. When you were asked: "And with respect to Pavlovic" -- and I'm quoting from page 47, line 12. "And with respect to Pavlovic, you and he were on friendly terms, like comrades; correct?" You said no. And now, three minutes later, you say that's what I told the Belgrade Court and that's the truth. So a consistent answer would have been yes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are not far away from the time. I think we have some 40 minutes left in view of your latest assessment, which was four and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. I was told 50 but that's quibbling a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 50 -- yes. No, you're right. As a matter of fact, my math is getting worse and worse. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That should work, Mr. President.
