I'd just wanted to mention that in respect of the Court's request to upload the document within 48 hours, the relevant excerpted pages from 65 ter 02406 have now been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter 02406a, which has been assigned P7357, and we uploaded six pages; that is, the speech that was shown, the Karadzic speech that was shown, and presumably the cover page as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar is hereby instructed to replace the current -- what is currently uploaded for P7357 to replace that by and it's a -- it's only there in -- it's there in two languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President, and it's under 65 ter 02406a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That -- what is presently under P7357 is replaced by 65 ter 02406a, and P7357 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, in view of the time I want to move on to a slightly different period, and that's a bit later in 1992. Now, referring back for a moment to your speech in Milici referring to 70 per cent held, 30 per cent not held among the parts of the region that by that time were not yet held by the Bosnian Serb forces was Cerska; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up P2095, I want to look at a Drina Corps order in November of 1992 referring to upcoming operations including, among other areas, Cerska. This is an order from the Drina Corps command dated 24 November 1992, in this case to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, pursuant to an earlier directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska of November 19, 1992, and it provides, among other things, launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. So, General, that was another reflection, in this case in November of 1992, to undertake further conquering of areas not yet under the control of the Bosnian Serb military and political authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an accurate document, but it is a consequence of major suffering precisely in this area. The political leadership from the area of Birac asked the supreme commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I don't recall asking you for the underlying reasons. But now that you're getting into them, let me ask you a question related to that. In fact, this operation reflected an effort to attain a key strategic objectives; that is, strategic objective number 3, the elimination of the Drina as a border; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no way. No. Do allow me to explain what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to allow to you explain. Now I have limited time and now we're going to focus on the questions that I'm putting to you. So your position is no way that this relates to the strategic objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this Trial Chamber has received evidence, and that's P356, e-court pages 146 through 147, it's also the same in the Serbian, that there was a meeting on November 8th of corps commanders, including General Zivanovic, whose order this is. And after Dr. Karadzic mentioned that it might be good if we solve the issue of the Drina, Mr. Krajisnik -- in fact, let's call it up. You can follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the portion that I was referring to, Mr. Krajisnik talking at that meeting: "I admire the military successes. It is very dangerous to seize their territories, the Drina and the Neretva." And then noting: "We have a disproportionate engagement of the army in relation to the strategic," turn the page, "objectives. We have not achieved the Neretva," that's number 4, "the sea," that's number 6, "and the Podrinje area," number 3. "We have achieved the corridor and separation with the Muslims." He goes on to note that the most pressing thing is to mop up Orasje," it's a Croat area, "and then to solve the problem of the Podrinje area and the Neretva river valley as soon as possible. The Muslims must not stay with us and they should not be given any kind of autonomy. The most important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic, the mopping up of the Drina," that is the "ciscenje" of the Drina. "The most important task is separation from the Muslims." Now, that's a meeting with the Bosnian Serb leadership, with General Mladic, the commander of the Drina Corps, that preceded both Directive 4 and the follow-up order from the Drina Corps that we just saw by General Zivanovic. It's crystal clear, General, is it not, that the -- that these directives which followed this meeting were an effort to do what the Bosnian Serb leadership ordered, and that is to achieve in this instance Directive number 3?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, just allow me. The political leadership of Birac asked, by way of an ultimatum from the supreme commander, to have this operation carried out because of the genocide that we experienced in Vlasenica, Srebrenica, and Bratunac. That was the basis. But you don't want to listen to any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you refrain from such comments. You were allowed to give an explanation and refrain from these nasty comments which you're supposed not to give as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you will agree that operations ensued in -- that took place in the first half of 1993 in the Podrinje resulting in the, quote/unquote, liberation of territory and that the taking of additional portions of Eastern Bosnia by the Bosnian Serb military; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were no operations in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Operation Podrinje 93, that is what it was called, but it's the consequence of what I spoke of a moment ago; namely, that the political leadership asked the supreme commander and the supreme commander issued an order to the commander of the Main Staff to carry out an operation because we had experienced a genocide that was never seen before. And I mentioned that from September until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you again. For one reason or another, you don't want to answer the questions. No one said -- you were not asked what the reasons were. You were just asked whether operations ensued in the first half of 1993 resulting in the liberation of territory. Whether that happened or not. Apparently by giving the reasons why it happened, although not part of the question, you apparently do not deny that these operations took place. Now that was what you were asked about. Again, you're -- by not answering the questions, you are really undermining your own testimony, and I think it would not be fair to the Defence that calls you as a witness to do that. Mr. Tieger, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we've heard now enough. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I have P338, please. Page 160 in the English; page 139 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take look at what the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership said in the combat readiness report in April of 1993 about these operations. And it's 160 in the English. Looking at the last sentence of the top paragraph in this document of April 1993: "In the last month and a half" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where can it be found in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be that it's the third paragraph from the bottom, the very last sentence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Could it be enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "In the last month and a half our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje as there by the strategic objective of our war would be realised, one that could be defined as 'establishing contact with Serbia on the river Drina or the Drina ceasing to be frontier.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's another reflection, General, of the fact that these operations were pursuant to and efforts to implement the strategic objectives which had been announced as early as May 12th, 1992. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me as commander, that is not true. I was not aware of any such truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you were aware of the fact that these objectives meant that the achievement of Directive number 3 meant that those areas identified in the November 24th, 1992, order that I showed you at the beginning of this session had to -- to be in Serb hands, areas like Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Gorazde, et cetera. You knew those had to be in Serb hands, didn't you, and you knew those were part of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As brigade commander, I received my task and my axis for the brigade, and that is how much I know. So we can talk about it in that framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you're not denying that that was the case, that the strategic objectives meant that areas, such as the ones I mentioned, were considered to be Bosnian Serb and had to become Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02380, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask a question. What we just looked at was the analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska, which analysis was done by the Main Staff of the VRS. Do you have any reason to challenge the accuracy of that analysis? So irrespective of whether you were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not up to me to evaluate the superior command or to give my opinion about the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you've given your opinion again and again, saying that what is written in this report is not true. So you have already done that. And therefore, I'm asking you whether have you reasons to challenge this analysis, and if so what those reasons are apart from that you have an opinion which differs apparently from why these operations were under taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be able to answer that question, I would have to read the entire analysis. Otherwise, I cannot take a position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The relevant portion was read to you. What the purpose or what the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even see that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was read to you. But if I say, "I need to read that paragraph," you could have asked, and Mr. Tieger would have given you an opportunity to do so. But he quoted at least that relevant portion. Mr. Tieger, perhaps next time we should be more careful that we verify whether the witness can follow the written text. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I thought because -- and I'd still maintain that because of the focus on identifying the precise portion in Serbian the witness couldn't have missed it, but we'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I even asked it to be enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 02380, e-court page 40 in the English and page 33 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The bottom -- toward the bottom of the page, we see Dr. Karadzic speaking. He says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you see where it starts recording what Mr. Karadzic said? It's the lower part of your text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "We cannot..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He notes that they still have not recognised our borders of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Gorazde is ours. Perhaps we will have to make some concessions in parts of Sarajevo itself for Gorazde to remain ours, because the Drina is of enormous importance for Republika Srpska and for the Serbian people and lastly it is one of the strategic aims for the Drina not to be a border, that is what we adopted here in this Assembly." Now, that's a reflection of the fact that the possession of the areas described in the November 24th, 1992, order, including Gorazde, are part of the -- are part of strategic objective number 3, which includes ensuring that the -- that the territory in that area is or becomes Bosnian Serb. That's what the Supreme Commander said, and that's the reality of the situation with respect to the strategic objectives. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't reach me what the Supreme Commander said. I knew my objectives: To protect the villages and to ensure normal life and work. That was the task of the brigade. As for the Supreme Commander and what the strategy was, that is something that I was not knowledgeable about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender this excerpt, Mr. President, under the same conditions as we discussed with the previously assembly session excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you reserve a number, awaiting the upload of an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number would be P7359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, General, let's take a look at how the liberation of the Podrinje referred to in the combat readiness report in April was implemented. And in that regard, let's call up 65 ter 03408 first. And what I will do is show you two or three related excerpts in order. There's no Serbian translation of this, so I will read it to you slowly, sir, and the Court and the Defence can follow along to ensure that the reading is accurate. This is a statement of the president of the Security Council issued on 3rd of March, 1993, regarding the situation in Eastern Bosnia. "The Security Council, recalling all its relevant resolutions and statements, expresses its grave concern at and condemns the continuing unacceptable military attacks in Eastern Bosnia and the resulting deterioration in the humanitarian situation in that region. It is appalled that, even as peace talks are continuing, attacks by Serb paramilitary units, including, reportedly, the killings of innocent civilians, continue in Eastern Bosnia. In this connection, the Security Council is particularly concerned about the fall of the town of Cerska and the imminent fall of neighbouring villages. The Security Council demands that the killings and atrocities must stop and reaffirms that those guilty of crimes against international humanitarian law will be held individually responsible by the world community." And, similarly, let me turn you to 65 ter 09352. This is an UNPROFOR report of 15 March 1993. Command UNPROFOR dispatch, focusing in this case on events in the area of Srebrenica. As you can see in the bottom of the third paragraph, it notes: "In visiting the town of Srebrenica the commander assessed that the town had been subject to continuous" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that. "... the commander assessed that the town had been subject to continuous bombardment and shelling until he arrived." Then if we continue to paragraph 6, it begins: "There is systematic cleansing of the Srebrenica enclave that has been going on full force now since at least the beginning of March and perhaps since early January. The Serbs are ethnically cleansing one village at a time. First by shelling the village, and then attacking with grounds forces." And if we continue toward the bottom of the paragraph in the penultimate sentence, it states: "Bratunac is reported to be cut off. Cerska and Konjevic Polje have fallen. Srebrenica is probably the next Serb objective which they could possibly take in the next three to four days if they so wished." General Andric, those two documents are reflections of how the operations to liberate the Podrinje were implemented; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two documents are not entirely true. The best truth will be provided will be by General Morillon who was there at a couple of meetings. Thanks to President Karadzic and General Mladic, the civilian population was spared from revenge. And as a soldier, I have to be proud of that. Thanks to the Supreme Commander Karadzic and General Mladic, we saved those civilians from revenge and retribution, and this is something that General Morillon can testify to. Otherwise, we enabled General Morillon to visit Srebrenica to bring aid there, to allow for the refugees or the civilian people to organise themselves, and to provide a transport for them to go to Kalesija. And we stopped at the entrance to Srebrenica upon the order of General Mladic. We could have captured it as early as the 15th of May, but thanks to an order by the Supreme Commander we stopped there. That's the truth, if that's what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, these documents, and in particular the first one I showed you, are just the tip of the iceberg of the unrelenting international pressure brought to bear on the Bosnian Serb leadership in the face of those illegal operations that forced the Bosnian Serb leadership to abort the intention to liberate the Podrinje in full and stop at Srebrenica. It wasn't a humanitarian gesture at all. It was a reflection of the reality of the pressure that was brought on them. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that this operation in 1993 was a military operation and had to be carried out because of Kamenica, where 120 people died. Because of Vlasenica, because of Milici. Had they been sitting there, nobody would have driven them away. But if somebody was killing Serbs every day, what were we supposed to do? Sit there with our arms crossed? They were killing us in 1941, 1942, and so we had to do something. Thanks to Karadzic and Mladic, no civilian casualties happened there. Even General Mladic said that the fighters must not be killed. They should have been allowed to go either to Kalesija or to Srebrenica, and General Morillon congratulated me a number of times. He said, "Well, done, Colonel. We did a good thing in making that sure that there were no casualties." And this is something that the public should be told at least. That's the truth. Please believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those two documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 03408 receives number P7360. And 09359 receives number P7361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no B/C/S translations yet, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first document should be MFI'd pending the translation, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7360 is marked for identification awaiting an English translation. P7361 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, is P7361 related to 65 ter 09359 or 09352?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 09359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 5-9, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At page 60, line 21, Mr. Tieger said: "And, similarly, let me turn you to 65 ter 09352."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, correction. And the document on the screen is indeed 09352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in our remaining time, let's take a quick look at some of your participation in those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up P2193.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know you've seen this document before, General. This is your report to the Drina Corps command of the 2nd of March, 1993, appearing to report basically that all is going well without major problems. And then reporting: "The village of Gobelji has been burnt. And tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine." Burning the village of Gobelji, General, was a way of ensuring that the Muslim inhabitants of that village would not return to that village and to that part of now Serb-controlled territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. If you need an explanation, I can give it to you. This is the duty operations officer, but that was a woman who was writing that report. Not the commander. It's a daily combat report. And the village has just eight houses. It had eight houses, but it was used as a fortified facility. So that was at the front line, the population was in Cerska. Only fighters went there to the line. And also, they took care of the cattle there. So this was a fortified front line such as the facility in Paljevine. And then in view of the fact that the woman is not sufficiently trained in the military sense, she said they burned, but she was actually angry because at the same day we had ten killed fighters. It says five here. And she said that it was burned. There was nothing to be torched there. This was a fortified military facility feature. The population was already in Cerska. So torching was not my objective. But last time I said that my father's house was also burned, so I knew what that meant to somebody. So I'm sure that the soldiers did not permit anything like that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, this report was sent under your name. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can see that there's no signature there. I was in action, so that operations officer would send a report out every day. I'm not disputing it, but I'm just saying that that was a girl who sent this report. She was a lieutenant. She drafted the report. What I'm saying, though, is that the village was not torched. The village practically didn't exist. It was just eight houses, and they were actually a fortified military feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you supervise this woman? She used your name. She was under your supervision. You were the commander. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the duty operations officer. I'm not disputing it, but the actual term. Secondly, I would like to say the torching continued. That's not true. This is TT840 feature. The torching did not continue. What happened was that the actual feature was being captured, but it's not a village. Torching is not -- did not continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you later correct your report when you found out that this was not a correct description of the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Combat actions continued, so this went to the Drina Corps command. Nobody had time to correct anything there. Actually, few understand the feature of Paljevine. We did not go on to that feature. It's a facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that way you accepted that your superior commands, the Drina Corps command, was informed in an incorrect way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that according to your duties as the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You accepted that your superior command was informed in a wrong way, and you didn't correct that. That was your responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a very factual question. You said Gobelji was just eight houses. Did those eight houses burn down or did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please believe me when I say that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, whatever you comments you give, you say have you no recollection of what actually happened. You explained to us that the whole report was wrong. At the same time, you say you don't know what happened, which puzzles me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you that it was a fortified military feature. I wasn't there personally. Therefore, now it would be superfluous for me to say that it was burned or not burned, if I hadn't been there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how would you then know that it was a fortified position, all eight houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I received a report from the subordinate unit commander whose task was to liberate the feature of Paljevine. There was a report from that feature of Paljevine that all villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm talking about Gobelji. Not at this moment about Paljevine. How did you know that Gobelji was a fortified position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a report from subordinate officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was a communication through a radio device. The communication proceeded via radio devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way you could suggest how we could verify whether such a report was given to you if there's no written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, only the commander of the unit that was carrying out actions in that area. Nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, the 1991 census indicates that 218 Muslims lived in Gobelji. Do you mind telling me how 218 people could live in eight houses?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information that it was only eight houses. Gobelji is a broader area. There are a number of villages there, but this was just eight houses. You can check that. It was just eight houses. Smrsanj over there is another village. But Gobelji has eight houses. According to my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you claim that this was all military necessity and not a case of trying to burn down as many Muslim houses as possible so that the Muslim population, which had been displaced, would not return to their villages. So I presume that the -- that your commander, the commander of the Drina Corps, would not have been exhorting his subordinates to burn as many Turk houses as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a purely military task and a purely military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P2192. This is an intercepted communication involving Drina Corps Commander Zivanovic, and as we see toward the bottom of the page, he instructs to hold tightly the positions and then asks: "Are the Turk [sic] houses burning?" He is told: "They are burning, they are burning." And then it says: "Way to go, as many as possible."

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not say what he said. I told you that I had a military objective and that I had 120 casualties from that area. Udrc, Paljevine. 120 civilians, women, fighters. Should we wait for more of our people to be killed? No. My military objective was clear and I had to resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly, General, I understand your assertion to be that the burning of Muslim houses was not about destroying their habitations so that the forceable displacement or cleansing of the Muslim population would be permanent, but you say it was about combat. It had nothing to do with who was living in those structures. So in that case --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims weren't living in those buildings at all. They were living in Cerska. They just had fortified buildings they were building. They were bringing livestock there. They didn't live there at all, but I have thousands of problems because from Udrc, Paljevine, and that feature they kept attacking innocent villagers. These were villages that they were attacking, so it was only natural. Now, what would a commander do? Just watch all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have P2194, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a March 1993 report to the Drina Corps command by Zvornik Brigade Commander Pandurevic, and in it as we see at the bottom of his report, he offers up the proposal: "We propose that houses should not be to torched when taking control of Konjevic Polje, but that they should be inhabited by people from Tuzla and other areas." General, that's a reflection of the fact that torching of what General Zivanovic exhorted as as many Turk houses as possible was about who was living there and what would be achieved by burning them, and General Pandurevic's suggestion that let's save those houses for the Serbs instead of burning them so Muslims can't return. That's clear from this document, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely support what Pandurevic said. And General Zivanovic, I don't know in which context he said that. So my objective is to keep whatever can be kept in order to move people in because we had lots of refugees. Over 180.000 people went in that area. We had lots of refugees from the Tuzla canton. And in Kalesija where I was born, we preserved all those villages. And thank goodness, Muslims returned and they live there to this day. Actually, my own village was burned after Dayton, and yet again people have returned. My strategy, my tactic was not torching. My strategy and tactic was to preserve my own people and to enable them to live and work normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After all that, sir, would you now please try to answer the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am answering. Now, I don't know specifically -- I mean, the gentleman asked me about Zivanovic's speech, and through the communications, and also about what Pandurevic said and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you was that -- it's a reflection of the torching that General Zivanovic exhorted as as many Turks' houses be as possible was about who was living there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll start again. The question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zivanovic was not talking to brigade commanders. He wasn't talking to me. He wasn't talking to Vinko Pandurevic. He was talking to some communications man. I don't know. So there was no influence in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please wait a minute and listen to the question. The question was: "General, that's a reflection of the ... torching ... General Zivanovic exhorted as as many Turk houses as possible was about who was living there and what would be achieved by burning them, and General Pandurevic's suggestion that let's save those houses for the Serbs instead of burning them so Muslims can't return. That's clear from this document, isn't it, sir." That was the question. Your answer, actually, is to say: Yes, it is clear, or no it is clear, or something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Zivanovic's conversation, you see that the reflection was efficacious because Colonel Pandurevic is saying the opposite: Let's protect houses. So that's what was done. Now, what General Zivanovic meant and who he was talking to, it wasn't certainly the brigade commanders. We, the brigade commanders, preserved the houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. [Microphone not activated] ... earlier explanation without answering the question. Yes, Mr. Tieger. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, but I have no additional questions for this witness. I would simply note that the excerpted portions or pages from 65 ter 02380 have now been uploaded under 65 ter 02380a, which has been assigned P7359. And we've uploaded the speech in its entirety, it's two pages plus the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7359 is admitted into evidence. And the speech was under the -- another number or is that the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was previously under 65 ter 02380 as part of a longer document. Part of the 33rd Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and we had reserved a number for that, I think. My colleagues are always better in the administrative matters. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all the same. It's not two documents. It's just one excerpt of one document. So the decision to admit has been pronounced. Witness, we'd like to see you back after 20 minutes when you'll be re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. At least, Mr. Stojanovic, if you have questions for the witness. Yes, you are confirming that. Witness, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, Mr. Stojanovic, you may have noticed that the witness has a certain inclination to move away from the question. Would you please strictly control that the witness remains within the scope of your questions. And could you give us any indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best, Your Honour. And I believe that we are going to finish by the end of the day. That is how I concentrated my questions for the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that effort. Mr. Andric, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Carefully listen to his questions and try to answer those. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, we will try to concentrate and finish by the end of our working today so that you don't have to stay until tomorrow and that is why I'm going to ask you to concentrate as much as possible. So let us go through what you were trying to say and what was said was that I should give you that opportunity. First of all, in your view, what was the reason why the command of the Drina Corps asked for combat and the liberation of the area of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, during the introductory part, I said that there was unheard of suffering in Vlasenica, Milici, Sekovici, Zvornik, Bratunac, Skelani, and I just referred to a short period from mid-September up -- or actually, until the end of September. I mentioned the victims. It was untenable. And the military and political leadership of Birac went to the supreme commander and asked by way of an ultimatum to resolve the issue of that area and to protect the Serb people. The supreme commander ordered the Main Staff for that area to be protected from constant attacks from the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, primarily Udrc, and so on. So the military operation was organised and we had to carry that out and I've already said why --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please speak a little slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But also come a bit closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the commanding officer of one of the units that took part that this combat, did you have intelligence concerning the forces of the enemy in that area?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire area of the 28th Division, about 10.000 armed fighters. According to the last report from January 1995, in Srebrenica there were about 35.000 inhabitants: 12.000 were military age, 10.000 were armed, 10.000 were local inhabitants in Srebrenica, and 10.000 from the different urban areas who had come to Srebrenica. And there were 1500.000 [as interpreted] who had come from other areas. So about 35.000: 12.000 military age, 10.000 armed. So I'm referring to the entire 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information -- please let us focus now on 1993. Did you have any information about the forces on the other side in the broader area of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is the Kamenica 5th Detachment, then the Cerska Detachment, Commander Hodzic who is from Vlasenica, then the Kasaba Detachment. The detachment of Konjevic Polje. In Cerska only there was brigade level, but Naser Oric sent his reserve of 800 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please call up 65 ter 09661.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can take a look, General. It's in front of you. That's a document of the command of the Drina Corps. The date is the 8th of December, 1992, and it is entitled: "Decision on the Liberation of Pobudje, Konjevic Polje, and Cerska." And in paragraph 1, the first part says that in the general Srebrenica, Zepa, Cerska sectors, and the Kamenica area, towards Zvornik, the enemy forces are rather strong and their number is increasing from 10.000 to 15.000 armed soldiers." In paragraph 4 of this order, it says: "In the Cerska area, the strength of enemy forces is up to 2.000 armed soldiers. They are deployed along the line and then the line is mentioned." This operative information and intelligence that the Drina Corps had, does all of this reflect the strength of the enemy in Cerska in December 1992 before the operation of spring 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I've already said for Srebrenica only 10.000, and I said in Cerska the equivalent was that of a brigade; that is to say, that a brigade is up to 3.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender 09661 into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number D1037.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, there were quite a few questions that pertained to your requests to have the question of the POW camp resolved. I wish to ask you whether, with a view to resolving the problem of POWs, you addressed the superior command - at that time, it was the Eastern Bosnian Corps - with a request to have that question resolved?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the request of the commander of the battalion, the 4th Battalion, I sent several requests to the superior command of the East Bosnian Corps. I remember the request from the 14th of June, then the request of the 17th of June, where I unequivocally ask that the prisoners be transferred to an appropriate area within the corps command. Brigade level is not in charge of a camp and is not entitled to a camp. It is a unit at corps level that can have a camp. So the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, issued an order on the 12th of June ordering the command of the East Bosnian Corps, but they did not do that. And then again on the 17th of June, he ordered that this question be resolved urgently and that POWs be relocated. And then after that on the 1st of July 400 prisoners, on the basis of our order, were transferred to the Batkovic camp. Then there was that report, 640. So 400 were transferred to Batkovic. Then on the 1st of July, also, 180 were released. Brought on a bus, taken to Kladanj. In the camp only 60 were left. And on the 3rd, my duty operations officer reported to the superior command that in the camp there were 60 persons left and 30 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. That we would allow to go towards Kladanj. And we said, "Please resolve the question of those prisoners as well," and that is that figure of 640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the witness referred to a lot of documents. If you have any of those documents, of course, we'd like to see them, and in which way to present them as evidence is another matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We'll try to go through these documents very fast. Could we please have P192 in e-court. I'll try, Your Honours, to identify and show as many of these documents as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if they confirm what the witness tells us, then if they're in evidence, then you could rely on those. But if you have any additional questions for the witness, of course, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we would hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, would you take a look at the document that is in front of you now. This is a document of the command of the Birac Brigade dated the 14th of June, 1992, and you say, in paragraph 2: "It is necessary to urgently resolve the issue of POW camps, because in Vlasenica, we currently have 520," if I can see this right, "prisoners. As for exchange, we have done nothing because there is no interest on the other side." Is that the document that you spoke of a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court P186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you said: "'... we currently have 520,' if I can see this right." It is not easy to read that, but in the English translation it says in handwritten words "640" in handwriting, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that we do have a problem with the translation, and will you see the next document that is precisely what I'm going to ask about. And you can go back to the B/C/S and you will see whether I -- actually, that's why I said if I see this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're looking at in a new document, actually, P186, and the date is the 17th of June, 1992. And yet again, from the command of the Birac Brigade, a telegram is being send to the command of the East Bosnia Corps, and you in paragraph 2, say: "It is necessary to urgently resolve the issue of the POW camps because in Vlasenica we currently have 640 prisoners." Is this yet another one of these documents that you spoke of a moment ago when I asked you about your requests for an urgent resolution to the question of POWs?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'd like to ask that we take a look at a document that is in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Its 65 ter number is 1D05389. 1D05389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, there was an addition in the lower part which was SR, which was translated as "independently." The Chamber has no idea what that means. If the witness could tell us. That was after your name. It was the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if I may ask to look at the previous document again, P186. P186.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you will see in the lower left-hand corner on the -- in the B/C/S version it says: "Commander Major Andric, Svetozar SR." What does that mean, SR? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Svojerucno," "signed in his own hand."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the translation should be revised. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 65 ter 1D05389 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document from the Bircani Brigade command of the 2nd of July, 1992. The heading is "Interim Operations Report to the Command of the East Bosnia Corps," where you say: "On the 1st of July, 1992, around 1700 hours, through our area of responsibility a column of vehicles passed with 180 refugees which was unloaded at the exit of our area of responsibility in the sector of S Luka, and the column proceeded on foot towards to Kladanj."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please be asked to repeat the rest of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you -- after you had read the content of the document, could you again phrase your question. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please provide an English translation, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Your Honour, unfortunately, we don't have it at this point. I would just like to tender this document or ask that it be marked for identification because it's a document that the witness referred to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the document you referred to, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the document that I referred to. There is another document from the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to this. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D1038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed. Awaiting a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart has a translation of that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if it could be provided to the Defence and uploaded together with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you the Prosecutor for his help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, we'll pass quickly through the documents. The next topic that I wanted to ask you about is something that was left incomplete, I think.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Did we show that document of the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there won't be any need for that because we have this document already.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because practically nobody was left in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the beginning of the question. The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you re-start your question because the beginning was not heard by the interpreters due to overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell the Court, did you at any point in time as the commander in the period of May 1992 have operational authority and command over the TO units in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that I never had any command over Zvornik units. The order that was mentioned of the 28th and the one of the 31st is something where you can see that the TO command was carrying out my orders, and they were asked to be sent to their superior in order to carry out co-ordinated actions in the Tuzla area. I state that with full responsibility. Nothing else is true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please look at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, while we're waiting for the document, the last line of what the witness said was not caught by the interpreters. However, a full answer is given already in the first line, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at document P3739 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document that you were shown in the cross-examination. The date is the 6th of June, 1992. This is a document of the command of the East Bosnia Corps, and the then-commander of that corps issues an order in paragraph 1 that all current TO Staffs are to be renamed into commands and units of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among other ones, the staff and the units of the Zvornik TO are referred here. You can see that under paragraph 2. So, please, according to your best knowledge, could you please tell the Trial Chamber at which point in time, if do you have such information, did the Army of Republika Srpska begin to function according to the system of unity of command in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really competent to talk about Zvornik since that was not part of my area of responsibility, but I will say that on the whole the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic, on the 21st, as the most responsible person, sent an organisational order for the formation of the Army of Republika Srpska. That was on the 21st. At the same time, mobilisation was declared. The mobilisation deadline was one month. And pursuant to this order, these staffs were to become part of the Army of Republika Srpska. Mobilisation was supposed to be carried out first and then units were to be formed; specifically, in my area of responsibility, I definitely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you there. You were asked about Zvornik, and you started saying that you are not competent to say anything about Zvornik. That was the question. If there would be any follow-up question, you'll hear that. You referred to the 21st. Could you tell us, 21st of what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 21st of May. That was when the Supreme Command issued the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The 21st of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will proceed slowly. And could you please complete this sentence, and I'm going to put the question to you now. When, according to you, if you know, did the Birac Brigade that you headed was placed under the unity of command system under the overall command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Birac Brigade spread over seven municipality. With a reduction of the area of responsibility, the brigade in its full capacity in late 1992 when the Drina Corps was formed started to function in its full capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document -- I apologise, Your Honours, I have 65 ter number, if -- I don't know if it has a P number. So it's 65 ter 32513.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, that's the map that you wanted to say something about at one point, and it was left for the re-direct. So I would like us to look at that now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, it's Exhibit P7355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic, it most likely has not escaped your attention that the answer the witness gave to your last question was after he'd [Realtime transcript read in error "I'd"] changed that question. But let's leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the right number is P7355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the record says that I changed the question, no, it was the witness who first changed the question and then answered his own question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is now document P7355, if I managed to note it down correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would like you to look at this map that's in front of you now. I would like to ask you this: What preceded the fighting around Kalesija and which incidents prompted the fighting in and around Kalesija?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that Kalesija was a Muslim majority area, numbering a total of 41.000 inhabitants and of which 7.500 were Serbs. Serb villages in the depth of the municipality of Kalesija such as Jeginov Luk and Dumica, Zolje Jajici, Sarska Basta [phoen], Brezik were already in March attacked by the territorials, i.e., the Muslims. Then a regular Yugoslav People's Army military column from the 4th Armoured Brigade was located at Dubrave. On the 4th of April -- actually, on the 7th of April, was blocked by paramilitary Muslim units and their weapons were seized. Then on the 17th of April, in Kalesija, the TO Staff commander, Kavalic [phoen] -- actually Karavelic came to Kalesija, formed units, and distributed weapons, 300 rifles. Then on the 3rd of May, a purely Serb village in the Kalesija municipality was attacked. This was in the urban area, purely Serbian village. And then on the 7th of May, Jeginov Luk was attacked just like it was in 1941. There were six armoured personnel carriers located there, and then paramilitary formations, Muslim ones from the Kalesija municipality, blocked the entire village, and they were asking for these armoured personnel carriers. The leadership of the municipality was forced to carry out a breakthrough in order to save the population. And then on 8th of May along the Memici-Kalesija-Dumica axis, Jeginov Luk also, fighting was conducted, Kalesija was liberated, and we reached those Serb villages. Meaning, on the 10th of May, we controlled Kalesija. On the 23rd of May, the Muslim forces took that back. And then the Serb municipality of Osmaci was left behind, and that was when these three villages were left that are mentioned, Like, Seher and Drvenica [phoen]. In those three villages, 300 inhabitants were left behind. And then we released the civilians through an order of mine. We left 120 people in the school in Paprace, then we put them in the gym, and then in the camp. And then luckily for me and luckily for those people, those people were exchanged so that all of them were practically exchanged. That is the real truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we don't have much time, General, please, a question. This line, this front line and the line of separation in the second half of 1992, 1993, until the end of the war, between the units of your brigade and the units of the 2nd Corps of the B and H Army was the result of set western borders of the Birac region or the results and successes and failures of units in that area of the front?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a result of success. On the 23rd, this was taken from us, placed under their control, and then our communications Zvornik-Osmaci were cut. We fought to liberate that village, practically, so that we could provide assistance to the civilian population. We didn't have any communications. They had blocked our roads. Therefore, that boundary was achieved in fighting and not in any kind of political decision or any other type of decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going finish with this topic with this question: The Serb villages that you mentioned in the Kalesija municipality, did they remain behind because of the way the front was set?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages remained behind, the houses were destroyed, the people were not there anymore. Unfortunately, those villages have now been occupied by the Wahabis who are going to do away with all of us one day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please begin his question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you re-start your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I really apologise to the interpreters. I don't have time. So can we please look at 65 ter 32499. English page 36, B/C/S page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, those are the questions that talk about your relationship with the Branko Popovic, alias Pavlovic, so that I would just like to clear that up too. You did give an answer the way it was recorded in the transcript. I'm going to quote that part of it, and you can follow along. First of all, asked by the Presiding Judge, what private professional contacts did you have, you answered: "Well, it was friendly" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please indicate where he is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we see what you're quoting from, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In B/C/S, I'm quoting the second and third line. In the B/C/S version. And I ask that in English, I think, I think, it's the previous page. Just one page before this. That was used by the Prosecutor, too. If I wrote this right, it should be page 36 in English. I think that was cut out and assigned its own number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that a selection was made which is supposed to include specifically the portion that Mr. Tieger put to the witness, and I think you intervened at that time and wanted to quote another part but still of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same page in B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to continue in B/C/S and I think that the next page is the one in English, and, again, the president of the chamber is asking you on the same page in B/C/S: "You just" -- and could I please have the next page in English. We're just going to wait for the next page in English. I think it's right now. The presiding judge is asking you: "You only -- you became friends having seen each other twice?" And your answer is: "Not friends but we talked as friends. We never -- I was not his superior and he was not my subordinate. How would we talk? I cannot talk as an officer, a superior and a subordinate." So now I ask you -- there is a bit of a problem here with semantics and the translation. Please do explain this and tell the Trial Chamber in your own words how you would describe this relationship with Mr. Pavlovic, from that period.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly. A man cannot be friends with a man if he has seen this other person only twice. Friendships are built over the years, but it's a fact that we talked in a friendly way. He was not my subordinate, I was not his superior, so in fact there was no reason for us to be enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm with some concern, looking at the clock. Also, in view of your earlier estimate in how much time you would use --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am finishing, Your Honour. With a request to put just one more question, as I've been asked by General Mladic. So I would like to conclude by doing that, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please say, General Andric, when you first had the opportunity to see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my great fortune that it was on the 18th in Han Pijesak when I arrived together with the political leadership from the area of Birac, and they reported saying Major Andric is here, he wants to go home or, rather, he wants to go back to his unit. He ordered -- he said execute him. He did not have me executed. I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber the 18th of which month and which year?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, thank you, on behalf of the Defence of General Mladic for the answers that you have provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, this is again inappropriate behaviour, waving from a distance, and it's just as inappropriate for you, Witness, to respond to that. And, Mr. Mladic, if -- Mr. Lukic, if you have any time ever, then explain to Mr. Mladic that if there's any question which is not triggered by the cross-examination, then it should have been put to the witness in examination-in-chief. Mr. Tieger, do you have any further questions? And I'm looking at the clock. I'm aware that if it's more than just one or two questions, and then I already feel guilty to all the interpreters and all those others who are assisting us that we would have to adjourn and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will try to do something very quickly, Mr. President, and see if it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, you commented a couple of times, I think the last time at page 81 of this transcript, to the effect that by, I think July or so, there were an extremely limited number -- I think you said practically no one left at Susica camp. You're aware of the fact, for example, that on the 20th of September there was a report to Major Simic of the commander of the East Bosnia Corps that there were 132 Muslim prisoners still in Susica; 130 men, two women. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't understand each other properly. Mr. Stojanovic did not place the report here so that you can see it. On the 3rd is stays that 60 stayed in the camp, the one of the 3rd of July. The 3rd of July. 60 stayed back and 30 civilians were released. We didn't understand each other well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apparently you are not aware that on the 20th of September that there was report that there was still 132 Muslim prisoners in Susica; 130 men, two women. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's in evidence, the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were confronted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave it at that for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you made a point of telling us about the formidable forces of the Muslims, a raid in eastern Bosnia in the latter part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could turn quickly to 65 ter 02364, page -- I think 104 in the English, is that right, and 95 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this would be your last subject, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Look to the bottom of the page in English, please. And you can look in B/C/S -- toward the top of the page of 95, look for the numbers 500-800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the English be scrolled down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is General Mladic addressing the Bosnian Serb Assembly and saying: "But please, I always tell people to think a bit, to put themselves in the shoes of our enemy. I ask you how would any of our military representatives, a representative of the authorities, a representative of any party, feel if he were at that bridgehead there, surrounded and with the river Sava behind his back. Or if he had to wait 50 or 100 hours for the ferry. What his morale be like? How would he feel if he were surrounded as are the Muslim people and its armed force" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "... surrounded as are the Muslim people and its armed force, if it can be called that, in Cerska, in Srebrenica, waiting for the transport to bring him 500-800 bullets." That's a reflection, sir, of the understanding of the situation at the time regarding the Muslim forces in Cerska and Srebrenica, as General Mladic said, if it can be called that, and their plight; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't know how these forces managed to kill so many Serbs. 120.000 in 1992. The Patriotic League had 120.000 military conscripts, according to the statement made by General Sefer Halilovic. Armed conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that excerpt, Mr. President, from the 23rd Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is there an excerpt that still should be selected or is this an excerpt already?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we still have to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could a number be reserved for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, this concludes your evidence in this case. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and that were put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise to all those who have assisted us, although I'm very glad that they were willing to continue. It's 14 minutes that we went beyond the time, but at least the witness could now leave and return home again. It's highly appreciated. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 30th of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of April, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
